A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so that the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. As soon as the manifest switches, browsers start requesting whatever names it lists. If any of those assets were still uploading, those requests would fail and pages would break. Uploading everything first means that when the switch happens, every file it names is already in place.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already fetched the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it named. Deleting those files would break pages for those users even though they did nothing wrong. Versioned names let the old and new sets coexist without colliding, so both the old and new manifests stay fully served.

Our releases happen in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those new names. The old assets stay where they are.

The upload comes first so the manifest never points at files that aren't there yet. If we switched the manifest first, any browser that fetched it before the upload finished would request new asset names that don't exist yet and get broken pages. Uploading first means that by the time anyone can see the new names, every file behind them is already in place. Versioned names make this safe: the new files sit alongside the old ones without overwriting anything, so uploading them has no effect on live traffic until the switch.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those browsers still hold the old names and will keep requesting those files. If we deleted them, those users would hit missing files partway through their session. Keeping the old assets lets every browser finish with the set it started with, while new visitors get the new release.

Each release uploads every new asset under a versioned name, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`, before anything references it. Only then do we switch the manifest to point at the new names.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the uploads finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request files that don't exist yet. That browser would get 404s and a broken page. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens, so the switch is effectively atomic.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch, from an open tab or a cached copy. They will keep requesting the old versioned files. If we deleted those files, those users would hit missing scripts or styles partway through a session. Because versioned names never collide, the old and new sets can live side by side. Each browser gets a complete, consistent set of files, whichever manifest it loaded.

Our release has two steps: upload every new asset under a new versioned filename (e.g. `app.3f9c2.js`), then update the manifest so pages point at those new names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that doesn't exist yet. If we switched the manifest first, any browser that loaded it before the upload finished would request the new filenames, get 404s, and render a broken page. Uploading first means the moment the manifest flips, everything it points to is already in place.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one. A user mid-session, or one with a cached page, still requests the old filenames, sometimes lazily, minutes later. If we deleted those files on release, those users would hit 404s for scripts, styles or chunks their page expects. Leaving them available lets the old version keep working until those sessions naturally move to the new manifest.

The versioned names are what make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so the two versions coexist and the manifest switch is the only thing that decides which one a fresh visitor gets.
